videos.title: dr elizabeth odera q&a session v1 (1080p)

segments.description: Welcome, coaches. It gives me great pleasure to introduce our live Q&A speaker today, Dr Elizabeth Odira. Welcome, Dr Elizabeth. Thank you so much for being here. It was hard for me to summarise your accomplishments and your accolades because they are significant, but a few really stood out to me and I'd like to read them out if I may. The opportunities that you've provided to over 5,000 children just through tennis alone is phenomenal. Over 2,000 children participating in that under-10 age bracket in the African Programme Schools Tennis for Better Health, and I know that was a really big part of your presentation that you pre-recorded. You've got close to 4,000 girls in Kenya alone involved in Girls Power Clubs. It's just phenomenal. The work that you've done in tennis and coming from a professional tennis background through academia and now into consultancy with sport and with corporate as well. I'm so glad to have met you. I'm really happy the coaches are able to listen in to your presentation and I'm super excited that we can ask you some questions today. So thank you so much for being here and sharing your information. Thank you. I'm really happy to be here. I think it's an honour and a great opportunity for me as well. That's delightful. For the coaches who are on board today, if you could take a look at the Q&A and your bottom panel and try and use that if you're interested in asking any

questions. But I will kick us off with one question. I wrote down a quote from your presentation. Liz, I started coaching because I wanted to change lives through improved health and education. So for me, that was just massive. To be able to change lives through coaching. Every child left every lesson with more life skills. And I was just hoping you could delve a little bit more into that and maybe give us an example of how you're able to achieve that. I think that when you are a coach, you're always a leader and you lead the lesson, but you know what it's like, especially with young children. They look up to you. They're excited about anything you show them. But they also are an open heart and an open mind. And this is the opportunity to actually point them in the right direction. They never get as much opportunity to learn so much from you. I learned and grew up learning from the coaches that taught me. They were not very many, but they were very effective in ensuring that I would become a better person. And because of that, I also picked up and learned to be able to do the same thing. There are things that happen around young people all the time that they need to know how to navigate through them. And through the game of tennis, it's very easy to give them the opportunity to express themselves and find answers. So that's why I think tennis is a perfect opportunity to use that.

Amazing. That's right. And for you to be able to layer that into the lessons, I think is exemplary as well. So your... Thank you. Sorry. I said thank you. Your presentation, it didn't really touch on this, but I was wondering if you could comment on this because a question has come through. And it's particularly important in Australia at the moment in all sports, not just tennis, that we see a very high drop off of girls, 14 plus. So around about 12, they start high school, but certainly in that 14 plus age group. What strategies have you come across that might be helpful in keeping these girls and women engaged in our sport? Most and foremost, being female myself, there are certain basic things that we realize is very important. In most cases, we don't like to be alone. We want to be in a situation where there are other girls as well. And especially the age group that we're talking about. It is difficult to engage girls if they're alone. They will eventually drop off. They like to learn and do things together. The second thing is often girls are very sensitive, especially in this day and age, when they think that they're being treated differently. So if I'll just give a very simple example. I've seen, I've had a coach who would coach everybody the single backhand, and then tell a girl, you can't do the single backhand. You have to do the double backhand. And she believes she's strong. She can do the single backhand. But that already gives her that,

oh, so you think I can't do it. So a lot of the times that the negativity comes from inside our own attitudes and what we learned in the past about young girls, without realizing that this is a completely different age. And I'm not talking about the age of the girl. I'm talking about the times that we're living in, where girls and boys think the same. And they both believe I can also do it. And then finally, I think one of the important things is, if you want to engage girls, try engaging them together. You'd be surprised to find that you can get a lot more done when they recognize that they will have someone else as well that they can relate to, even if they will, at the end of the day, compete against each other. It does bring the more girls you have, the more girls you will have. I mean, you know, the more girls walk in, the more chances you will have in having girls who actually stay in the programs. That's just keeping it simple. Yep. And those things that you've mentioned, they're all very achievable. So it's very similar in Australia. We can do, we can try and do those things as well. Thank you for that response. For me, another question that that popped into my mind and your presentation, it was so clearly as it was, it provided clarity that perhaps when you're starting out in your career, that you might follow the goals of the business that you're working for. But at some stage, you really need to have a personal goal. And that personal goal

met us to you, because that's going to drive you, it's going to ensure that what you do on a day to day basis is important and keep you involved. But when, when and how do you find that balance? I can imagine as a younger coach, that would be quite hard to do, because you're quite often being told what to do. When do you think younger coaches can, can find their own goals? Or how does that come about? Do you think? I think it's not about when. And it's, it's more about why not. You want to be able to, to get up in the morning and already have a certain personal goal for yourself when you're stepping onto that court. Something simple that makes it possible for you. First and foremost, when you're talking about young people, they are extraneous things that happen around them at the club. You're already being in your mind being pushed to do some things and not quite in the same way. And sometimes I've tried to encourage young people to also find a way to quietly push back. And I'm giving that as an example. So it, there must be something that you know you're pretty good at. Use that to find a way to push back. So you can suggest, for example, oh, yeah, during the warmups, would you mind if I handle the warmups and added a little bit of my thing in it? And, and, and then from there, they start to say, okay, let her do the warmups. Well, let him do the warmups, whatever it is. And, and after a while,

you start to, they start to build confidence in you doing more. So it's, it's about picking you learning, starting to pick things that will eventually become a strength for you. It's about finding simple ways to push back and to start growing individually. So that there is something that stands out about you within that organization, even though you're not in charge. Amazing. So that notion of empowerment as well, that comes into, into play there, if they can take ownership and get some confidence and therefore. In fact, use the right word, taking ownership. Yes, absolutely. I also love the way you use the word serving. So serving people, serving the community. And, and that really stood out for me as well. Coaches perform a service to a chosen community. And, and I guess it's a similar vain question in a younger or a coach who might be newer to the industry. Is it, is it when they find their passion that they find their community or their people or what your examples were wheelchair tennis or perhaps, you know, youth tennis or maybe girls in tennis. Do you think younger coaches should try coaching a whole range of different communities and then find their passion? Absolutely. It's, it's important to, to have, to be able to say later that I tried that, you know, I tried that. It wasn't really my thing, but I did try it. I didn't go out there. So be brave enough to say I'll try it, even if it's just once. But I'm going to step out there because you may

be surprised to find that that is exactly where you needed to be. And when you're young, anything is possible. It should be that anything is possible. So yes, reach out, take that step, get that experience and then be able to say, I tried it. Maybe it wasn't my, for me. Or I tried it and actually I can do this. And perhaps even try something that makes you feel a little uncomfortable. I'm sure there's a few times you've had some roadblocks, Liz, in your career that you've had to push past and try new things. Oh yeah. I think some of them are experiences that you get when you're much younger and you hope that you'll never have to go through that again. If I can give an example real quickly. I was, I grew up at a time when tennis was really a white person's game. And the tennis clubs are always, and it's probably the same in Australia. All the nice, big, amazing tennis clubs are always in places that there isn't any public transportation. You have to have a car. I had to find ways to get there. And one of the clubs was in an area where there were wild animals. So in the evenings, you would find it very difficult to get there. And I had to be able to go there and play tennis and play a tournament. First of all, it's very difficult to be able to get into the club that would make you wait at the gate because they don't know. They didn't even understand what is that young black girl doing,

hanging out there at the road and holding a tennis racket and thinking she can play tennis. So after that, you get to play at the late hours or you play when the sun is at its highest. Always something was always wrong. But I said, if I'm playing against somebody else, that person is also suffering as much as I am. So I'm just going to stick it. And for some reason, I stayed. I stayed because I wanted to prove to myself. It didn't matter who that other person was, but I wanted to prove to myself that I'm stronger than this and be able to go back. So every time I set a new goal, if I'm late, this is what I'm going to do. If I'm that kind of thing, so I will walk. I work out which direction is the best direction to get to the bus stop. And I'll try it this time. Next time, I noticed there's a dog that passes me every time and is always barking at me. I'm going to make friends with that dog and the dog will escort me to the bus stop. And you just keep finding all sorts of very funny things. And you find yourself talking to yourself and laughing. But the experience, eventually I said one day I'll be able to turn around and tell people, do you know this is what happened to me? And the most amazing thing is that about 30 years later, I became the head pro at that same club. And it was, I loved the fact that I was able to make changes there. But the one thing that made me, I know this sounds dumb, but made me feel I had my power back. It was the day that I was doing so

well, but I walked out and said, I'm giving you notice. I think I have proved to myself that I'm good enough. I don't need to work here. I do have, I know people who I can introduce and are ready to take off and will do probably even a better job than I can. But I'm satisfied. I reached my goal. So it's just, being young is just a number. But the goals that you set for yourself, just so that you can make a difference, remember to yourself too. Matters. And it could take years or it could just happen tomorrow. But it's important that you stay on them. Absolutely. So once the positive outlook that shone through that answer and that example was amazing. And the fact that you even influenced a tennis club for the better, your own career, yourself, and then provided an opportunity for someone else is phenomenal as well. So a question from that is, have you ever lost your passion? And if so, were you able to find it again? Were you able to find a way to get it back? Or have you just sort of shifted from one challenge to the next, looking for something else that burns the fire within you? Are you talking about passion for tennis? Passion for tennis. Passion for challenges in life. It seems like you will rise to any occasion. So it's moving from one challenge to the next, either tennis or life. Some of the things that a coach, including young coaches, but generally coaches face is especially coaches who work hard to build

players, is that the players move on. And it sometimes can be some of the most painful and difficult moments for you, especially when you're just about to, you're at the crux where you're just about to help that player turn the corner. And then the player walks away. And I've seen and experienced that myself, where you've taken the player through, you work together with that player, and the player has gone on to play big tournaments, and then you're sitting there during the tournaments. You can't tell somebody, don't talk to that person. I'm just giving an example. And eventually, very quickly, they have moved to a different coach. The problem was not that they moved. The problem was that they moved at that moment, just when they were about to turn the corner and be really good. But they believed that you don't have what it takes to take them to the next level. And the worst thing for me was not that they moved to the other person, but that I knew the chances were very low that they were going to be able to make it. Not because the coach was bad, but because the way that people learn, that particular player learns, was did not, at that time, did not require interruptions. And that interruption did affect that player in the end. And they started losing really badly. And for me, that was the saddest thing that they didn't have enough. Initially, I thought, oh, so you don't have confidence in me. And then I

realized it has nothing to do with you at all. And I'm sure the other young coaches to go through that, other coaches who have the same experience. So you almost say, what's the point? And then you later realize it has nothing to do with you, but it's a most unfortunate incident. So the nothing to do with you then helps you provide context when you're bouncing back from that challenge? Yeah, everybody has their journey. And sometimes they just have to take it. And they have to learn their own lessons. And you have to step back as a coach and say, okay, this is it. So here's a quite a structured question. The concept around positive youth development, competence, confidence, connection, character, as coaches, is enough importance placed on the connection and character development as mentors? No, not enough. And whoever asked that question has asked a very beautiful question, because it's very important that we recognize that mentors have such a strong influence on what we later become. And that there's not enough of them, the right kind of mentor, and especially for young players, if they don't find the right one, they will find one. And it may be the person that they will imitate may not be the kind of person that you would have hoped they did. And character building is so critical because it then helps the player succeed as a player, but also as a human being. Because at the end of the day, you are human. For those who have gone on tours with players

and seen what happens, you begin to realize that the character of players is so important for them to be able to survive the circuits and be able to be successful at the end of the day and become successful humans too. That people can imitate and safely say, yeah, I'd love to be like you. And you truly are my champion. And there are so many tennis coaches that would be mentors without even knowing it, to younger players, the coaches in the teams, the community as well, particularly in regional areas, they are absolutely mentors to the community. So that's really important. And I'll let the question ask and know that it was a great question. So thank you for answering that one. You were talking about coaches as builders in your presentation. So they're building a player, they might be building a community, they're building themselves as well. For yourself, who's achieved so much, how do you go about still growing as a coach and a leader considering all the successes that you've had? There is no such thing as completion. I think it's a revolving thing. So you go up to the top and then you come back around to pick up either pick up something you've never quite did or someone that you want to be able to turn the corner with. And usually that's how I counted that. For example, these days I coach just a limited number of players, but it's important for me that I keep doing that. And I always include a few young people who are below six years,

which people find really hilarious because they're like, but you're already coaching at a higher level. But that's where the beauty is because they look up to you and they think you're just everything. But at the same time, you're looking at them and thinking, do you know you are everything? You have so much potential in you. I just love to see what you are in the future. And you work together and learn from them every day. There's so much you can learn. I love the sessions that we go through. And they always come back to teach me something new that I didn't know before. And I teach them something new that they didn't know before. And you just keep having that revolving thing. So I have learned strange things about what young people eat and how they combine together. And I've tasted some of it and almost puked. But then others I've looked at and I've been like, who came up with this combination? Yes. And then I've learned about the games that they play, that I never got a chance to play. And a lot of it is online. And they are incredible games that learn life skills that actually can be applied on the tennis court. And it gets them engaged and you keep working. So they teach you and you teach them. It's a brilliant combination. So there is never a chance, there's never a no chance opportunity where you're like, I'm only just going to be the one applying myself. If you're like that,

then your tennis sessions are dead because you need to also open up your mind and your heart and learn from those that you're trying to teach. Then you'll have a successful session. No, that's brilliant. You provide so much clarity. Just the concept is that nothing, we're not complete. There's always a way to learn. It's cyclical. You might have a time where you're the mentor. You might have a time when you're the mentee and being mentored by a six-year-old, which I love that concept, Liz. I think that's exciting for the future as well. If you could give a coach starting out three top tips, what would they be? Ooh, that's a good one. I think a first and foremost, step out saying, every morning saying, I'm here to learn. Then the second thing is I'm here to give the best that I have. I'm here to give the best of me. The third one, I'm here to lead. Amazing. When you're there with those three, you know that every time you go and say that I'm there to lead, it means that you planned. You planned your session. You didn't just walk in and do the same old, same old. You're also there to learn. You know that there's something new that you're going to discover about those that you're working with. I'm not saying the ones you're teaching. I'm saying the ones you're working with because as you are leading them, they're also showing you how they want to be better so that when you lead, you lead with those pointers that they're giving you. I know

that I will leave this place better because I will have picked up something from them. That's brilliant. Thank you, Liz. I really appreciate your time today on our live Q&A session. I think that together with your presentation, the coaches can learn so much about working with players and working with their team, finding their communities to serve and finding themselves along the way. I think it's a beautiful concept and a different way of looking at things. I would like to encourage the coaches that they will receive a survey monkey and in that, they have a chance to win one-on-one sessions with yourself. If they're interested in those, they need to make sure they complete that survey monkey. I certainly thank the coaches for their time today. They've invested their time to watch the presentations and also to come in and listen to you, Liz, which has been brilliant. We certainly look forward to working with all the coaches this year, 2022. We're fingers crossed that we can have a great year and perhaps you can get back to Africa on that plane ticket that's been begging for the last couple of years. Thank you. It's been a great opportunity. Thank you. It's been our pleasure. Have a lovely day.
